newsitem.title: USA: Space station stumbles, but no chance of demise.
newsitem.headline: Space station stumbles, but no chance of demise.

text.p: When it comes to the International Space Station, critics say money shouts and science whispers.
The controversial programme, first envisioned in 1984 and redesigned repeatedly since then, came under fire last week because of newly announced delays pegged to Russia's problematic participation.
But even one of the project's harshest congressional critics acknowledged it will go forward, largely due to the piles of dollars -- and yen, francs and lire -- already spent.

"Sure, the space station is going to happen, because the United States has paid $18 billion," Representative James Sensenbrenner, a Wisconsin Republican, said on Friday, "to walk away from the programme at this point in time is simply to throw the huge investment away and nobody can responsibly say that's what they want to do."

Sensenbrenner also noted high expenditures by Japanese, European and Canadian partners in the project. According to the Congressional Budget Office, the European Space Agency has spent $2.79 billion as of the end of 1996; the Japanese space agency has spent $2.12 billion; Canada has spent $812 million and Italy has spent $800 million.
But none of the modules paid for with these funds will orbit without a crucial Russian service module for the current space station version, and this has turned into a headache.

Wilbur Trafton, NASA's Associate Administrator of Space Flight, told a congressional panel last week that the Russian Space Agency needs about $140 million in the next two months to keep service module construction on track for launch in December 1998. That is already a delay from the previously planned launch in early 1998.
Trafton said the agency wanted to take $200 million from the Space Shuttle budget to pay for contingency plans and an additional $100 million to help the Russian programme.
Confidence in Russia's space capabilities is not running high in Washington, especially in light of difficulties encountered by the Soviet-vintage station Mir.

The 11-year-old Mir has had many problems in recent months including a fire and the loss of its main oxygen generators. Most recently a cooling system developed leaks, and fumes from leaking coolant caused breathing problems.

"Russia is never going to pay for its obligations (to the international space station) and the rest of the world is going to have to complete it without the Russians," said Sensenbrenner in a telephone interview.
For some, though, the question is whether the station is worth building at all.

The National Aeronautics and Space Administration insists the project will be an orbiting laboratory where microgravity would aid in biotechnology experiments as well as research into how humans and other life forms react to low gravity.

But Robert Park of the American Physical Society told lawmakers these goals have largely been reached through research on the U.S. space shuttles and Mir. In essence, he said, research has shown that humans' sense of balance is disturbed in weightlessness, and bones get more brittle.

Ursula Goodenough, a biologist at the University of Washington in St. Louis, said the station would not contribute greatly to the development of new drugs based on protein crystals, as some scientists have claimed. For example, Goodenough said, protease inhibitors, formed from crystals and used in the fight against AIDS, were developed on Earth.
In testimony before Sensenbrenner's panel, Park said he had yet to hear one positive statement about the station by any scientist who was not directly involved in it.

Park said the United States should use the expected seven-month delay caused by Russia to re-evaluate the project. "If this is simply an exercise in international cooperation, we should say so and drop the pretence of scientific research," Park said.
